as_told: A woman sees Pablo Picasso in a restaurant and asks him to sketch something on a napkin. He draws for a few seconds and asks for a large sum. When she says it took him only seconds, Picasso answers that it took him forty years.
lesson: Fast work by an expert rests on many years of learning, so its value is not the minutes it takes.
what_happened: No record from Picasso's life (he died in 1973) tells this story. The earliest telling found is in Mark H. McCormack's 1984 business book 'What They Don't Teach You at Harvard Business School', page 169, where it is told as a story without a source. A similar exchange did happen to James McNeill Whistler: at his 1878 libel trial against John Ruskin, he said that he asked two hundred guineas for a painting made in two days not for the labour but 'for the knowledge of a lifetime'. Whistler printed this exchange under his own name in 1890.
false_part: No record shows that Picasso ever made this napkin sketch or gave this answer; the story first appears in print in 1984, eleven years after his death.

earliest_telling.where: What They Don't Teach You at Harvard Business School (Bantam Books, 1984), p. 169
earliest_telling.quote: the  story  about  the  woman  who  approached Picasso  in  a  restaurant,  asked  him  to  scribble

original.what: Whistler's own printed account of his cross-examination at the Whistler v. Ruskin libel trial (November 1878), in his book The Gentle Art of Making Enemies
original.quote: “No;—I ask it for the knowledge of a lifetime.”

original.what: The punch line of the 1984 McCormack telling (Open Library full-text snippet of page 169)
original.quote: "No,"  Picasso  said.  "It  has  taken  me  forty  years  to  do that."

lesson_verdict.why: A major review of expert performance found that top performance in most fields follows at least about ten years of intense practice, so quick expert work does rest on long learning. Whether a price should follow from this is a matter of judgement that no study settles.

source.what: Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer (1993), 'The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance', Psychological Review 100(3): 363-406, abstract
source.quote: extended for a minimum of 10 years.

confidence_note: The McCormack text is quoted from Open Library search snippets, not from a full saved copy of the book. No telling before 1984 was found, but Google Books, HathiTrust and newspaper archives were not searched. That Whistler's exchange inspired the Picasso story is likely but not proven. The Ericsson review supports the 'years of learning' part of the lesson; later work (for example Macnamara and others, 2014) finds that practice explains only part of skill differences.
